data.title: Neurofibromatosis type 1 — viva
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Neurofibromatosis type 1** (Genodermatoses)_

**Q1. Define NF1 (von Recklinghausen disease).**
- Autosomal dominant neurocutaneous disorder (1 in 3000) due to loss-of-function NF1 gene mutations (17q11.2) encoding neurofibromin — a RAS-GTPase activating protein (tumour suppressor); ~50% new mutations; complete penetrance with variable expressivity

**Q2. Revised NIH diagnostic criteria (2021).**
- ≥2 of: ≥6 CALMs (>5 mm prepubertal, >15 mm postpubertal); axillary or inguinal freckling; ≥2 neurofibromas of any type or 1 plexiform; optic pathway glioma; ≥2 Lisch nodules or ≥2 choroidal abnormalities; distinctive osseous lesion (sphenoid wing dysplasia, anterolateral tibial bowing, pseudarthrosis of long bone); heterozygous pathogenic NF1 variant (≥50% VAF in normal tissue)
- Child of a parent meeting criteria needs only one feature

**Q3. Describe the cutaneous features.**
- CALMs (first sign — infancy), freckling (Crowe's sign — axillary/inguinal, 3–5 years), cutaneous neurofibromas (soft, skin-coloured to violaceous, 'button-hole' sign — invaginate on pressure; appear at puberty, increase in pregnancy), subcutaneous neurofibromas (firm, along nerves, painful), plexiform neurofibromas (congenital, 'bag of worms', overgrowth, risk of malignant change), juvenile xanthogranulomas (with risk of JMML), naevus anaemicus, glomus tumours, pruritus

**Q4. Systemic features and complications.**
- Eyes: Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas — >90% adults), optic pathway glioma (15% children — visual loss, precocious puberty)
- Skeletal: scoliosis, sphenoid wing dysplasia, tibial pseudarthrosis, short stature, macrocephaly, osteoporosis
- Nervous: learning disabilities/ADHD (~50%), epilepsy, aqueductal stenosis, brain tumours (gliomas), unidentified bright objects on MRI
- Vascular: hypertension (renal artery stenosis, phaeochromocytoma), moyamoya
- Malignancy: malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour (MPNST — 8–13% lifetime; pain, rapid growth, hardening of plexiform neurofibroma), GIST, breast cancer (women <50), JMML, rhabdomyosarcoma, phaeochromocytoma

**Q5. Classify neurofibromatosis.**
- NF1 (classic), NF2 (bilateral vestibular schwannomas — merlin, 22q; now called NF2-related schwannomatosis; few CALMs, cataracts, meningiomas), schwannomatosis (SMARCB1/LZTR1), segmental (mosaic) NF1, Legius syndrome (SPRED1 — CALMs + freckling, no neurofibromas)
- Riccardi classification (8 types) — historical

**Q6. Histopathology of a neurofibroma.**
- Unencapsulated dermal tumour of loosely arranged spindle cells with wavy 'S-shaped' nuclei in a pale myxoid/collagenous stroma with mast cells; S100 positive (Schwann cells), CD34 fibroblasts

**Q7. Management.**
- Multidisciplinary yearly review: skin, BP, growth, development, scoliosis, eyes (annual ophthalmology up to 8 y), neurology; MRI when symptomatic; genetic counselling (50% transmission)
- Cutaneous neurofibromas: excision, CO2 laser, electrodesiccation (cosmetic/symptomatic)
- Plexiform neurofibromas: selumetinib (MEK inhibitor — approved for symptomatic inoperable PN in children ≥2 y), mirdametinib (newer); surgery
- MPNST: wide excision, radiotherapy; whole-body MRI surveillance in high-risk; breast screening from 30 y in women

**Q8. Describe neurocutaneous syndromes (PYQ).**
- Phakomatoses: NF1, NF2, tuberous sclerosis, Sturge–Weber, von Hippel–Lindau, ataxia-telangiectasia (oculocutaneous telangiectasia, ataxia, immunodeficiency, lymphoma; ATM), incontinentia pigmenti, hypomelanosis of Ito, neurocutaneous melanosis, PHACE, epidermal naevus syndromes, Klippel–Trenaunay, Wyburn-Mason

**Q9. Genetics of NF1.**
- Autosomal dominant, complete penetrance but variable expressivity; ~50% new mutations; NF1 gene on 17q11.2 encodes neurofibromin (RAS-GTPase activating protein — tumour suppressor); loss → RAS/MAPK overactivity (basis for MEK inhibitors); segmental (mosaic) NF1 when post-zygotic

**Q10. What is a malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour (MPNST)?**
- Sarcoma arising in a plexiform neurofibroma in ~8–13% lifetime; warning signs — persistent pain, rapid growth, change in consistency (hard), new neurological deficit; FDG-PET/MRI and biopsy; treatment — wide excision, radiotherapy; poor prognosis

**Q11. Which skeletal features occur?**
- Scoliosis (dystrophic, early, rapidly progressive), sphenoid wing dysplasia (pulsating exophthalmos), long-bone bowing and pseudarthrosis of tibia (congenital), short stature, macrocephaly, osteoporosis, non-ossifying fibromas

**Q12. Describe surveillance in a child with NF1.**
- Annual examination: skin, growth, head circumference, BP (renal artery stenosis, phaeochromocytoma), spine (scoliosis), development/learning (ADHD, learning disability), puberty (precocious puberty from optic glioma); annual ophthalmology till 8 years for optic pathway glioma; MRI only when symptoms; breast cancer screening in women from 30 years

**Q13. Selumetinib — what and when?**
- Oral MEK1/2 inhibitor approved for children (≥2–3 y) with symptomatic inoperable plexiform neurofibromas — reduces volume and pain; side effects: acneiform rash, paronychia, GI upset, raised CK, ocular (retinal) toxicity; mirdametinib also approved recently (confirm availability)

**Q14. What are the types of neurofibromas?**
- Cutaneous (dermal) — soft, sessile/ pedunculated, 'button-hole' sign (invaginate on pressure), appear from puberty, increase in pregnancy
- Subcutaneous — firm, tender nodules along peripheral nerves (higher MPNST risk)
- Plexiform — congenital, diffuse, 'bag of worms', overlying hyperpigmentation/ hypertrichosis, can cause disfigurement and overgrowth; ~10% MPNST lifetime
- Spinal/ internal neurofibromas

**Q15. What is the button-hole sign?**
- Pressing a soft cutaneous neurofibroma pushes it into the dermis through a defect felt like a button-hole; it pops out on release — differentiates from other soft tumours (lipomas, skin tags)

**Q16. Describe the eye findings in NF1.**
- Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas — >90% adults), optic pathway glioma (15% children, usually <7 y — visual loss, proptosis, precocious puberty), choroidal abnormalities (bright patchy nodules on NIR imaging — newer criterion), plexiform neurofibroma of eyelid (S-shaped lid), glaucoma, sphenoid wing dysplasia

**Q17. What are the neurological and cognitive features?**
- Learning disabilities (~50–60%), ADHD, autism spectrum features, macrocephaly, epilepsy, hydrocephalus (aqueductal stenosis), headaches, 'unidentified bright objects' (T2 hyperintensities) on MRI, optic glioma, other gliomas (brainstem), Moyamoya

**Q18. What tumours are associated with NF1?**
- Optic pathway glioma, other gliomas, MPNST, gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST), phaeochromocytoma, carcinoid (duodenal somatostatinoma), juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia (with JXG), rhabdomyosarcoma, breast cancer (women <50 — screen from 30 y), glomus tumours of digits

**Q19. What is the relationship between NF1, JXG and JMML?**
- Children with NF1 and juvenile xanthogranulomas were once thought to have a markedly higher risk of juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia; current evidence suggests the added risk is small — routine haematological screening is not mandatory, but examine for hepatosplenomegaly and check CBC if symptomatic

**Q20. What is Legius syndrome and segmental NF?**
- Legius: SPRED1 mutation — CALMs and axillary freckling, macrocephaly, learning issues but no neurofibromas, Lisch nodules or tumours; genetic test differentiates from NF1
- Segmental (mosaic) NF1: features confined to one body segment from post-zygotic mutation; risk of transmitting full NF1 if gonadal mosaicism

**Q21. NF2 — key differences.**
- NF2 (now 'NF2-related schwannomatosis'): NF2 gene (merlin) chromosome 22; bilateral vestibular schwannomas (hearing loss, tinnitus, imbalance), meningiomas, ependymomas, juvenile posterior subcapsular cataract; few CALMs, cutaneous schwannomas (plaque-like); bevacizumab for vestibular schwannomas

**Q22. Describe the management of cutaneous neurofibromas.**
- Surgical excision of symptomatic/ disfiguring lesions, CO2 laser/ electrodesiccation for multiple small ones, radiofrequency ablation; MEK inhibitors (selumetinib) shrink some cutaneous neurofibromas — topical MEK inhibitors under trial; psychological support

**Q23. Pregnancy in NF1.**
- Neurofibromas may increase in number and size; higher risk of hypertension, pre-eclampsia, caesarean delivery; prenatal or pre-implantation genetic diagnosis available; 50% transmission risk

**Q24. Cardiovascular features.**
- Hypertension (essential, renal artery stenosis, phaeochromocytoma, coarctation), NF1 vasculopathy (stenoses, aneurysms, Moyamoya), pulmonary stenosis (also Noonan overlap — NF1–Noonan syndrome)

**Q25. Histopathology of plexiform neurofibroma vs MPNST.**
- Plexiform: tortuous expanded nerve fascicles with myxoid stroma, S100/SOX10-positive Schwann cells, CD34+ fibroblasts
- MPNST: hypercellular fascicles of atypical spindle cells, mitoses, necrosis, loss of S100/SOX10 and H3K27me3

**Q26. How do you counsel parents of a child with NF1?**
- Explain AD inheritance (50% risk to each child), variable severity even within a family, regular annual reviews, signs needing urgent review (vision changes, new pain, rapid lump growth, headaches, precocious puberty, BP rise), school support for learning difficulties, NF support groups

**Q27. What is the role of mosaic and NF1 microdeletion syndrome?**
- Whole-gene 17q11.2 microdeletion (5–10%): more severe — earlier and more numerous neurofibromas, facial dysmorphism, intellectual disability, overgrowth, higher MPNST risk
- Missense 'p.Met1149' or 'p.Arg1809' variants — mild phenotype without neurofibromas (pigmentary only)

**Q28. Differential diagnosis of multiple neurofibroma-like tumours.**
- Multiple lipomas (familial lipomatosis), schwannomatosis (painful schwannomas — SMARCB1/LZTR1), Proteus syndrome, Cowden syndrome, multiple endocrine neoplasia 2B (mucosal neuromas), multiple dermatofibromas, cutaneous leiomyomas (Reed syndrome)

**Q29. What is the prognosis/life expectancy in NF1?**
- Life expectancy reduced by ~10–15 years mainly due to MPNST, other malignancies, and vascular disease; most patients live productive lives with surveillance

**Q30. Why is NF1 called a RASopathy?**
- Neurofibromin is a RAS-GAP; its loss increases RAS-GTP and downstream MAPK/ mTOR signalling — like other RASopathies (Noonan, Costello, cardiofaciocutaneous, Legius); explains overlapping features and use of MEK inhibitors

## Quick spotter facts
- CALMs + axillary freckles + neurofibromas + Lisch nodules — NF1
- Button-hole sign
- Selumetinib for plexiform neurofibroma

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Neurofibromatosis); NIH 2021 revised diagnostic criteria. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
